newsitem.title: UK: Britain sets new limits for inflation target.
newsitem.headline: Britain sets new limits for inflation target.

text.p: Britain's Labour government, keeping up its vigorous pace of economic reform, reaffirmed its tough inflation target on Thursday and said the Bank of England would be called to account if the goal was significantly undershot or exceeded.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown told parliament he was setting a target of 2.5 percent for annual underlying inflation (RPIX), the same as that of the previous government.

But in a letter to Bank of England Governor Eddie George, Brown said that if the measure -- which excludes volatile home loan payments -- diverged from the target by more than one percentage point in either direction, he would expect a public letter from George explaining why.
Dismissing earlier speculation by economists, Brown said the new structure did not mean he was setting a new target band for underlying inflation of 1.5 to 3.5 percent.

"The thresholds do not provide a target range," Brown said in his letter to George. "Their function is to define the points at which I shall expect an explanatory letter from you because the actual inflation rate is appreciably away from its target."

Brown told parliament that his latest move, which follows his decision last month to give the central bank freedom to set interest rates, made monetary policy "more rigorous and more open." He stunned British finanical markets with that move within just days of taking office following the Labour Party's landslide May 1 election victory.

"It is the best guarantee that we can have of the consistently low inflation which has eluded us as a country, as a platform for what everybody wants, which is high and stable of growth and employment."
The Bank used its new powers at the first opportunity last Friday, raising official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent.

Critics of Brown's decision to let the central bank set rates had argued that monetary policy would be tighter than it needed to be in future, which would lead to slower economic growth and job losses.

A Treasury source said the new structure had twin goals -- removing the threat of deflationary monetary policy while sending a signal that fighting inflation was the goal of both the government and the Bank.
"We want to avoid a deflationary bias. It is easy to deflate an economy," the source said.
The decision made clear that the new government wanted a U.S.-style arrangement whereby the central bank must bear down on inflation but also ensure healthy economic growth is maintained.
Some City economists were unimpressed, saying the new structure represented a loosening of the anti-inflation stance.

"The apparently strict monetary policy regime that was unveiled a month ago is now being diluted," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe. "The key point is that the inflation 'cap' has been replaced by a spot target."
Financial markets took the announcement in their stride.
British government bonds were a little higher and the FTSE-100 index of leading shares was up about 33 points on the day at 4,757.

Nonetheless, the new framework leaves some question marks. The previous Conservative government first set an inflation target about five years ago, laying down a range of one to four percent and targeting the mid-point -- 2.5 percent.
But the wider range was gradually forgotten and by the time Kenneth Clarke -- Brown's predecssor -- became Chancellor in 1993, the inflation target was widely viewed to be 2.5 percent or less.
Underlying retail price inflation finally fell to 2.5 percent in April this year and stayed at that level in May, according to official figures released on Thursday.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, was sanguine about the changes.
"It amounts to a slight softening of the inflation target, but I think there was a need for some lower limit to prevent the BoE from going into overkill on interest rates," he said.
"I don't think it's going to result in significantly higher inflation than we'd otherwise have seen."
